\subsubsection{Accuracy}\label{sss:eis-accuracy}

A known \SI{11.000}{\kilo\ohm} resistor reads \SI{11003}{\ohm} at
\SI{0.000}{\degree} --- \(+0.029\,\%\) --- flat from \SI{0.1}{\hertz} to
\SI{1}{\kilo\hertz} at the bottom gain code, and \(+0.030\,\%\) at
\SI{5}{\kilo\hertz}. On an electrode the error is set by the noise gain
\(1 + R_f/|Z|\) at the frequency being measured, not by the electrode's
chemistry (Figure~\ref{fig:eis-error}): the fresh case at gain code 63 is the
most accurate of the three below \SI{100}{\hertz} at \(0.005\,\%\) and the worst
above \SI{1}{\kilo\hertz} --- \SI{2.8}{\percent} at \SI{5}{\kilo\hertz}, and
\SIrange{1.84}{3.68}{\percent} across the corner set ---
because its impedance falls from \SI{999}{\kilo\ohm} to \(R_u\) across the sweep
while \(R_f\) does not move. Gain-ranged to the lowest code in compliance and
with no calibration applied, the channel holds \SI{0.44}{\percent} of magnitude
and \SI{1.04}{\degree} of phase from \SI{0.01}{\hertz} to \SI{20}{\kilo\hertz}
on all five loads, \SI{0.33}{\percent} and \SI{0.29}{\degree} at and below
\SI{5}{\kilo\hertz}, and \SI{0.030}{\percent} and \SI{0.010}{\degree} at and
below \SI{1}{\hertz}. Ranging badly costs an order of magnitude: the worst code
still in compliance reads \(+0.43\,\%\) on the calibration resistor at dc where
the best reads \(0.029\,\%\).

\paragraph{Measured through the converter.} An \SI{11.000}{\kilo\ohm} load at
gain code 20, excited by the reference ladder and read through the input
multiplexer and an extracted converter, demodulates from \num{256} converter
codes --- \num{64} per excitation period at \SI{13.587}{\kilo\hertz} --- to
\(+0.343\,\%\) of magnitude and \SI{-2.94}{\degree} of phase against the
small-signal analysis of the same load and gain code. Three demodulations of
that one record separate the terms: the analog nets give \(+0.126\,\%\) and
\SI{-0.013}{\degree}, reading them at the conversion apertures adds
\(+0.855\) points and \SI{-2.882}{\degree}, and decoding the codes takes
\num{0.638} points back off. \textbf{The converter's whole cost is one number.}
Its incremental gain is \num{628.00} codes per volt on the current channel and
\num{624.04} on the potential channel, which swings over \(12\times\) less of
the transfer curve; a ratio cancels a common gain exactly and a different one
not at all. That \(+0.636\,\%\) mismatch predicts \(-0.632\) points against the
\(-0.638\) measured, leaving \num{0.006} points for quantisation, dither and
aperture together. \textbf{The converter is a two-point gain calibration, not a
noise floor.}

\paragraph{The phase error is the excitation grid, not the converter.} One
converter serving two channels samples them half a conversion apart, and point
sampling then quantises the two-level excitation's edges onto two grids that
differ by that half conversion. The cost is \(180\,f/f_s\) degrees ---
\SI{2.81}{\degree} at this frequency against the \SI{2.94}{\degree} measured.
Three measurements fix the mechanism: a sinusoidal excitation on the same
interleaved grid returns \SI{0.0000}{\degree}, rotating the interleaved answer
at the apertures by \(180\,f/f_s\) leaves \SI{0.08}{\degree} of residual, and
two records taken on one grid measure \SI{0.08}{\degree} on the other side of
zero. \textbf{Against the \(\pm\SI{0.573}{\degree}\) gate
an uncorrected interleaved read is capped at \SI{2.77}{\kilo\hertz}},
\num{0.0032} of the conversion rate. The rotation is deterministic and needs no
calibration; a stepped sine removes the term outright and two records on one
grid cost twice the record time.

\paragraph{What limits accuracy, in falling order.} First the uncalibrated
feedback capacitor: on the fresh electrode at gain code 63 and
\SI{5}{\kilo\hertz} a stored dc feedback resistance costs \SI{3.8}{\percent} of
magnitude and \SI{15}{\degree} of phase on top of the loop's own
\SI{2.8}{\percent}, because it ignores the pole the \SI{22}{\pico\farad}
compensation capacitor puts in the feedback impedance. Measuring a known
impedance at every frequency and taking the ratio removes that term entirely ---
\SI{2.33}{\percent} at the same point, below the loop error itself, the two
errors partly cancelling. Second, the reference-electrode tap: through real
converter codes, demodulating the commanded potential instead of the
electrode's own reads \(+2.934\,\%\) where the tap reads \(+0.343\,\%\), so
\textbf{the tap is worth \num{2.59} percentage points of magnitude}. The
small-signal figure for the same comparison is \SIrange{0.02}{0.2}{\percent}
and it is superseded rather than contradicted: an ideal excitation source makes
the commanded potential exact by construction, so that figure carries A1's loop
error alone and none of the ladder's own code-pair error, which reaches
\SI{3.5}{\percent} (Section~\ref{sss:eis-excitation}). Third, a magnitude
mismatch between that calibration impedance and the load: a \SI{999}{\kilo\ohm} load calibrated against
\SI{11}{\kilo\ohm} at the same gain code carries a fixed \(-0.27\,\%\), exactly
the difference of the two loop errors (\num{0.278} against \(0.003\,\%\)). At a
fixed process point that is a correction; across a wafer it is a spread, and the
requirement below. Last, the loop error itself, which scales exactly with the
noise gain: \num{0.120}, \num{0.330}, \num{0.660} and \SI{1.322}{\percent} at
\(R_f/|Z| =\) \num{7.3}, \num{20}, \num{40} and \num{80}.

\paragraph{Across corners the error spans a factor of two.} It is monotone in
the amplifiers' transconductance, so \SI{85}{\celsius}
is the worst point of the set for every load and every gain code and the slow
corner the best: the calibration resistor reads \SIrange{0.023}{0.041}{\percent}
about its nominal \(0.029\,\%\), and the typical electrode at gain code 20 and
\SI{1}{\kilo\hertz} spans \SIrange{0.70}{1.40}{\percent} over the process corners
and \SIrange{0.88}{1.46}{\percent} over \SIrange{0}{85}{\celsius}. Temperature is
the larger axis, and the two do not add, because the fast corner and
\SI{85}{\celsius} lie at the same end. Phase moves far less: the fresh case at
gain code 63 and \SI{5}{\kilo\hertz} spans \SIrange{4.57}{4.79}{\degree} where
its magnitude error doubles, because phase is set by pole positions and this
corner set does not move them --- for the same reason it does not move \(R_f\),
which is the caveat of Section~\ref{ss:eis}.

\paragraph{Across a wafer the spread is the feedback resistance, and it is
process rather than mismatch.} At the bottom gain code, \num{500} samples give
\(\sigma = \SI{10.91}{\percent}\) with process variation alone and
\SI{0.43}{\percent} with mismatch alone, against \SI{11.12}{\percent} with both
over \num{654}; the two add in quadrature to \SI{10.92}{\percent}, inside the
third measurement's own interval. At gain code 63 the same quantity is
\SI{12.13}{\percent}, and the fresh electrode's \SI{2.8}{\percent} at
\SI{5}{\kilo\hertz} becomes \(2.99 \pm \SI{0.96}{\percent}\). The poly sheet
resistance moves all four channels of a die together, so no amount of averaging
removes it and a single measurement does; what a single measurement cannot
remove, the channel-to-channel residual, is that \SI{0.43}{\percent}. That orders
the ways firmware can turn two converter readings into an impedance. \textbf{A
stored nominal resistance law is unusable as a calibration constant}: it puts the
whole spread on the answer --- \(\sigma = \SI{10.2}{\percent}\) of magnitude at
gain code 0 and \SI{12.3}{\percent} at code 63, the bottom-code run's own
\num{649} dies reading \(-32.1\,\%\) to \(+30.6\,\%\) below the feedback
pole --- on top of the
\SI{9}{\percent} nominal offset the law already carries at the bottom code.
\textbf{One dc measurement of the feedback resistance per chip removes
essentially all of it}: \(\sigma = \SI{0.0006}{\percent}\), four orders of
magnitude better and indistinguishable from measuring the current at every
frequency, which is the bound and would need a current reference the die does not
carry. That is a fourth independent reason for the calibration impedance. Phase
escapes the argument entirely --- the feedback resistance is a real scale factor,
so the stored-law and dc-calibrated architectures report identical phase in every
case measured, and a chip with no gain calibration at all still reports phase to
the accuracy above.

\paragraph{The calibration impedance must be switchable across decades.} Against
a standard matched to the load, the ratiometric measurement reaches the bound
above in mean and in \(\sigma\) at every frequency, and beats it at dc where the two loop
errors are identical and cancel outright: \(\sigma = \SI{0.0002}{\percent}\)
against the bound's own \SI{0.0006}{\percent} on the typical load and
\SI{0.0056}{\percent} on the fouled one, with non-overlapping intervals. Against a standard \num{9.2} times away
in magnitude it instead \emph{injects} spread, \(\sigma = \SI{0.18}{\percent}\),
\num{300} times worse than the dc calibration it replaces. Above the feedback
pole, where a dc calibration cannot help at all, it is the only thing that does:
on the fresh electrode at gain code 63 and \SI{5}{\kilo\hertz} a stored dc
resistance gives \(6.85 \pm \SI{1.88}{\percent}\) and the ratio
\(2.51 \pm \SI{0.83}{\percent}\) even against a standard \num{91} times away ---
\num{2.7} times less bias and \num{2.3} times less spread. The fixed
\(-0.27\,\%\) above is therefore a distribution,
\(-0.26 \pm \SI{0.11}{\percent}\), and matching the calibration impedance to the
decade being measured is a requirement on the hardware, not a refinement of the
firmware.
